prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

my old friend I wonder how far north you travel? The road goes west starting two doors up from the Dog’s Bollocks ending at sunset. So many sunsets Facebook and Instagram couldn’t contain them. So many yellow lines, white stripes there’s hardly a Valiant left to defy them. Now the years overtake us. Visits as a boy to Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy in their K’Rd council flat led me to the greatness of the great north whipping its dusty tail up to the skyline of Reinga. Yet why do I see your darkness as silence my friend? You’re a sleek black eel pumping blood all the way to Karekare, to Muriwai, to Bethells, to Piha, and our vehicles surf the surges back to K’Rd, back and forth, LOL, rocking up our shock absorbers and surfboards. Keep bringing the waves Great North Road. Keep saving the whales! Keep the toheroas shining tucked away from spades in sandy bolt-holes. Smile in your cars and honk honk honk on the Great North Road.

outputs.L1:
My old friend, I wonder how far north you travel. The road runs west, beginning two doors up from the Dog’s Bollocks and ending at sunset. So many sunsets that Facebook and Instagram couldn’t contain them; so many yellow lines and white stripes that there’s hardly a Valiant left to defy them.

Yet why do I see your darkness as silence, my friend? You are a sleek black eel, pumping blood all the way to Karekare, Muriwai, Bethells, and Piha. Our vehicles surf the surges back to K’Rd—back and forth, LOL—rocking our shock absorbers and surfboards.

outputs.L2:
Old companion, how deep into the north do you run? Your westward course begins two doorways beyond the Dog’s Bollocks and stretches toward the setting sun—more sunsets than Facebook or Instagram could ever hold. Yellow markings and white bands cover you so thoroughly that scarcely a Valiant remains willing to challenge them.

Time now speeds past us. When I was young, I visited Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy in their council flat on K’Rd, and those journeys revealed the grandeur of the Great North, flicking its dust-covered tail toward the distant outline of Reinga.

But, my friend, why does your darkness feel like quietness to me? You are a smooth black eel, driving blood outward to Karekare, Muriwai, Bethells and Piha. Our cars ride your swells back to K’Rd, again and again—LOL—jolting shock absorbers and surfboards alike.

Great North Road, continue to deliver the waves. Go on protecting the whales. Let the toheroa gleam safely in their sandy hideaways, beyond the reach of spades. Grin from behind the wheel and sound your horns—honk, honk, honk—along the Great North Road.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the Great North Road as an old friend—a familiar route stretching westward from the city toward Auckland’s wild coastal landscapes. Their connection to it began in childhood, during visits to relatives living in a council flat on Karangahape Road. From those early encounters grew an enduring sense of the road’s scale and grandeur, as though it offered a passage from the dense urban centre to the open horizons of the Tasman Sea.

The road is portrayed as a dark, living artery, carrying generations of people and vehicles toward Karekare, Muriwai, Bethells, and Piha. Repeated journeys between Karangahape Road and the west coast become intertwined with memories of surfing, physical movement, family, and changing seasons. Each trip retraces a familiar path, yet also marks the passage of time, allowing past and present to overlap.

At once nostalgic and celebratory, the reflection honours the Great North Road as more than a transport route: it is a link between city and coast, childhood and adulthood, memory and landscape. Yet this celebration also carries a sense of responsibility. The speaker calls for the protection of whales, toheroa, and the fragile coastal environment, reminding us that the places reached by the road must be cherished and safeguarded for the future.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents Auckland’s Great North Road as far more than a route through the city. Through nostalgic memories and vivid descriptions, it becomes a symbol of movement, connection, and continuity. The speaker recalls the road with affection, suggesting that it holds traces of past journeys, changing neighbourhoods, and generations of people who have travelled along it. These memories give the landscape emotional depth, linking personal experience with the wider history of Auckland.

Personification makes the road appear alive. It stretches through communities like an enduring artery, carrying people between the city and the western suburbs, bush, and beaches. Rather than remaining a passive feature of the landscape, the road seems to witness change, absorb stories, and participate in the life around it. This image emphasises its importance as a shared space where urban life, human relationships, and the natural environment meet.

References to Auckland’s western beaches and surrounding communities broaden the poem’s focus beyond the road itself. The imagery evokes the distinctive character of the west: rugged coastlines, powerful seas, native bush, and settlements shaped by their closeness to nature. The road connects these different places, creating a continuous passage from crowded urban areas to open and untamed landscapes. In doing so, it brings together contrasting aspects of Auckland’s identity.

The passage of time is central to the poem. Although people, neighbourhoods, and environments change, Great North Road remains a familiar and lasting presence. Its endurance allows it to serve as a link between past and present, preserving memories even as the city develops around it. The poem therefore celebrates the road’s cultural and environmental significance, portraying it as a living record of Auckland’s history and a vital connection between its people, places, and natural world.
outputs.L5:
### The Dog’s Bollocks

In British slang, **“the dog’s bollocks”** describes something exceptionally good—the very best of its kind. Despite its crude wording, the phrase is usually intended as enthusiastic praise. A stylish new car, an outstanding meal, or a brilliant performance might all be called “the dog’s bollocks.”

Context matters, however. The expression is highly informal and may offend in polite or professional settings. Among friends, though, saying, “That was the dog’s bollocks,” simply means: “That was absolutely excellent.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem addressed to Auckland’s Great North Road, blending childhood memories, west coast beaches, traffic imagery, social media, and environmental concerns.
counterfactuals.output:
Great North Road, you were the first long sentence I learned by heart, beginning in the city’s bright throat and running west through suburbs where the dairies smelled of newsprint, milk, and hot pastry. From the back seat I watched your power poles flick past like metronomes, counted red cars, held my breath under bridges, believed every green light was a blessing meant especially for us.

You carried us toward Piha, Muriwai, Karekare—names dark and shining as wet stones. Beyond your brake lights and petrol rainbows, the Waitākere ranges lifted their green shoulders, and the road narrowed into fern-shadow and pōhutukawa. Then came the beaches: black sand burning our soles, salt whitening our eyebrows, the Tasman throwing its whole iron body against the land. We built fortresses below the tide line and were astonished when the sea took them.

Now I meet you through a windscreen crowded with warnings. Traffic glows red ahead, a rosary of impatience. Buses sigh, trucks grind uphill, cyclists balance beside the gutter’s broken glitter. On my phone, friends post sunsets from Lion Rock, drone shots of surf, reels of foam folding perfectly onto shore. We give the ocean hearts while it rises. We scroll past slips, flooded streets, stranded birds, rāhui, smoke from summers that have forgotten how to end.

Great North Road, you remember when our parents drove with paper maps spread across their knees, when the west seemed far enough to be wild. But no place is far now. Tyre dust enters the streams. Plastic arrives before us at the beach. The kauri stand behind cleaning stations and warning signs, their roots vulnerable to what we carry without knowing.

Still, you lead us there—through rain on glass, through lanes that merge and unmerge like arguments, through billboards promising new lives on cleared hillsides. You are asphalt, artery, archive. Under your patched skin lie tramlines, footsteps, streams made to vanish. Above you, notifications flare and fade like small artificial stars.

Great North Road, old road, restless road, teach us another way to travel: not as owners rushing toward a view, but as guests entering a living house. Let us arrive with less. Let us listen past the engine. Let the children in the back seats look up from their screens and see the ranges breathing, the gulls writing white commas over the surf, the sea returning—again and again—to revise the shore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental ode to Great North Road in the voice of someone reminiscing about visits to relatives in a Karangahape Road council flat and journeys north toward Cape Reinga.
counterfactuals.output:
**ODE WITH A NORTHBOUND SPINE**

Great North Road,  
you were never one road—

you were a long thought  
beginning under the bruised neon of Karangahape,  
where the council flat held our relatives  
six floors above the buses,  
above the dairy’s blue milk-light,  
above men calling to one another  
as if the night were a deep valley.

The lift shuddered up.  
The lift shuddered down.  
Someone had scratched a name into its steel door  
and every visit I watched that name  
open  
and close.

Inside: boiled cabbage, talcum powder,  
a mantel clock refusing the century.  
Aunties made tea strong enough to stand in.  
Uncles leaned from the balcony  
and pointed west—

There, they said.  
That’s the road.

*

O Great North Road,  
old tramline, ridge-line,  
tarred-over memory—

you carried us past Grey Lynn’s villas  
with their damp lace curtains,  
past the zoo’s hidden roar,  
past Avondale horses running  
through the sleep of Saturday.

Mum packed sandwiches in waxed paper.  
Dad tested the tyres with his thumb.  
We children became knees, elbows,  
hot vinyl, orange peel,  
the endless argument of whose turn  
to sit by the window.

NORTH, said every sign.

NORTH, said the bonnet,  
bright with sacrificed insects.

NORTH, said the radio,  
losing one station, finding another  
in a burst of weather.

*

Beyond the city, the road kept shedding names.

It became motorway,  
became highway,  
became a black ribbon worried  
between paddocks.

At Brynderwyn the engine prayed uphill.  
Whangārei shimmered in petrol heat.  
Kawakawa arrived wearing Hundertwasser colours,  
and toilets became a pilgrimage.

Farther on, pōhutukawa leaned from the coast  
like red-handed witnesses.  
Kauri stood inland  
holding centuries upright.

We crossed rivers whose names  
the adults spoke carefully,  
then carelessly,  
then carefully again.

Every bridge said:

leave something here.  
Every bridge said:

take something with you.

*

At night in the motor camp  
the sky came down close enough  
to hear us breathing.

Our relatives remained behind  
in the Karangahape flat—  
their kettle clicking off,  
their curtains silvered by traffic,  
their balcony facing all that distance.

Yet they travelled with us:

in the thermos,  
in the cardigans folded for weather,  
in the warning not to swim after eating,  
in the biscuit tin rattling  
at every cattle stop.

Family is a road that insists  
it is a room.

Family is a room  
with wheels under it.

*

Then Cape Reinga—

though the older name waited there too:  
Te Rerenga Wairua,  
the leaping place of spirits.

We stood where the seas met  
and would not become one.

Tasman: dark shoulder.  
Pacific: pale hand.

Below, the water argued in two languages.  
Wind emptied our mouths of speech.  
The lighthouse kept its small white counsel.

No one told us what to remember.

So I remembered everything:

the lift’s metallic cough,  
the aunties’ tea,  
the long back seat,  
the road unspooling through rain,  
the last tree gripping the cliff  
with roots like fingers.

*

Great North Road,  
you begin whenever I turn back.

You run from that council balcony  
to the farthest headland,  
from fluorescent hallway  
to salt-white sky.

Even now, I travel you in pieces:

K’ Road after rain.  
A chipped cup.  
A service station moon.  
A hand asleep on a suitcase.  
The sea meeting itself  
and breaking.

O road,  
O relative,  
O long unfinished sentence—

take me north again,

not to arrive,

but to feel the whole country  
leaning through the wind,

calling every lost name  
home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal, stream-of-consciousness monologue personifying Great North Road as an old friend and a black eel carrying cars toward Karekare, Muriwai, Bethells, and Piha.
counterfactuals.output:
Great North Road, you old liar, you old friend, you black eel with a spine full of lamps, swallowing cars at dusk and carrying them west in your slick belly—one toward Karekare, where the waterfall keeps falling through its own memory; one toward Muriwai, where the gannets stitch white weather to the cliffs; one toward Bethells, black sand breathing under bare feet; one toward Piha, Lion Rock crouched in the surf, dreaming of thunder.

I have known you since you were narrower than regret. You used to knock at the window with rain on your coat and say, Come on, there’s still some daylight left, though we both knew daylight had already packed its gold suitcase and gone.

Your traffic lights blink like tired eyes. Green, you remember me. Amber, you almost remember me. Red, you hold my face between your wet hands and ask why I stayed away so long.

But I never stayed away. I was in every tyre hiss, every service-station coffee trembling in its paper cup, every child asleep in the back seat with the ocean already roaring inside their head. I was the loose coin under the handbrake. I was the map folded wrong. I was the voice saying left, no, right, no, follow the smell of salt and crushed fern.

And you, old road, kept swimming.

Past shops lit like aquariums. Past houses with their small square moons. Past paddocks where the cows stood ankle-deep in fog, solemn as drowned librarians. You flexed your tar-black body under us, scale after scale of rain, carrying our little metal prayers toward the Waitākere dark.

Do you choose who arrives?

Do you whisper Karekare to the lonely, Muriwai to the restless, Bethells to those who have misplaced their names, Piha to the ones who need the sea to shout louder than they can?

You only laugh in gravel. You only shrug your shoulders into another bend.

At night I imagine you uncoiling from the city altogether, dragging intersections, letterboxes, dairies, and sleeping suburbs behind you like seaweed. By dawn there is nothing inland but your shining trail, and all of Auckland has been delivered to the coast—cars nosed into black sand, headlights staring at the waves, everyone silent at last.

Then you turn your ancient head.

Your eyes are two roundabouts full of stars.

Get in, you say.

Where are we going?

West, you say, as if west were a place, as if west were a person waiting barefoot beyond the ranges, as if the sun had not drowned there every evening since the beginning.

So I climb into your mouth.

You taste of petrol, rain, and old promises.

And away we go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary New Zealand prose poem that mentions the Dog’s Bollocks, K’Rd, Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy, Valiant cars, surfboards, whales, and toheroa, ending with drivers honking on Great North Road.
counterfactuals.output: At the Dog’s Bollocks the bass leaks into the wet midnight of K’Rd, where the dairies shine like small promises and everyone is waiting for a bus, a break, a message from home. Uncle Bruce still talks about Valiant cars as if they were weather—big, temperamental, impossible to forget—while Aunty Lindy keeps old photographs of surfboards stacked beside the bach, noses pointed toward a sea that once seemed endless. Out beyond the breakers, whales shoulder through the dark, carrying their low songs south; beneath the sand, toheroa hold fast to their secret tides. Morning comes in a hi-vis vest, with coffee, cranes, and gulls tearing open the city’s soft rubbish bags. We move inland through rain, past villas and tyre shops, past all the lives we nearly lived, while the light changes and drivers honk on Great North Road.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a nostalgic, playful tribute to an iconic Auckland road, using vivid local geography, repeated references to sunsets and waves, road markings, aging, humour such as “LOL,” and an ecological plea.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Ode to Tāmaki Drive**

Oh, Tāmaki Drive, you salt-streaked ribbon,  
curling from the city toward the pōhutukawa glow—  
past Ōkahu Bay, Mission Bay, Kohimarama,  
all the way to St Heliers, where the old sea walls know.

Sunsets on the windscreen, sunsets in the tide,  
sunsets turning Rangitoto into a purple sleeping giant.  
Waves slap the rocks—*kia ora, kia ora*—  
then leap at cyclists, LOL, cheerfully defiant.

Your white lines fade; your yellow lines grumble.  
Bike lanes appear like bright new veins.  
Road cones breed overnight near Kelly Tarlton’s,  
while buses sigh through sudden rain.

We grew older beside you—  
knees less springy, cars more dented,  
ice creams smaller, parking more mythical,  
every “quick swim” extravagantly extended.

Still the waves keep waving.  
Still the sunsets spill gold.  
Still Maungauika guards the harbour mouth  
with stories older than old.

Tāmaki Drive, don’t lose your blue-green heart  
to exhaust, plastic, runoff and haste.  
Give the shellfish clean water, the seabirds safe sand;  
leave no bottle, tyre, or takeaway waste.

Let the pōhutukawa lean. Let the little blue penguins pass.  
Let cyclists, walkers, buses and wheelchairs share your shore.  
For sunsets return, and waves return—  
but some things, once gone, return no more.

So here’s to your bends, your cracks, your painted arrows,  
your joggers, dogs, scooters and Saturday tribe:  
Auckland’s beloved, weather-beaten front porch—  
forever young, forever aging,  
forever Tāmaki Drive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
